public_notes.title: Schools And Community Persistence
public_notes.text: The Tribe's history dates a community-funded subscription school to 1859. It describes state permission for a separate school system in 1911, revocation in 1913 and later reinstatement after community organizing. Its account describes the East Carolina Indian School serving Coharie and other Native students in 1943, with the original building later becoming Tribal administrative offices. These are milestones in education and institutions within a continuing people.

public_notes.title: Reconnecting With The River
public_notes.text: The Tribe's river page describes storms blocking access to the Great Coharie River and volunteer work beginning in 2015. It connects that work with memories of fishing and returning river access across generations. The page also states a future clearing goal and hoped-for partnerships. Those remain stated aims in this source; current ecological outcomes and access conditions have not been independently verified.

public_notes.title: A Government In The Meadows
public_notes.text: The Tribe's official site places its government in Hollister, in the area it calls the Meadows, and describes a council chosen by Tribal citizens. This profile follows that specific government's public account. A fuller historical timeline still needs additional own-published sources. The site's copyright years are not a founding date for its people or government.

public_notes.title: Education And Cultural Continuity
public_notes.text: The Tribal School page states a mission integrating American Indian culture with academic learning, technology and community involvement. Red Earth describes cultural learning for all ages and lists possible activities rather than a guaranteed current timetable. The Tribe also publishes its scope for government consultation around development and cultural heritage. These are self-described purposes and processes; outcomes and class availability have not been independently measured.
